question.es: Al cruzarse con los peatones en esta vía, ¿qué distancia lateral debe dejar?
question.en: When approaching pedestrians on this road, what side-by-side distance should you leave?

text.es: 1,5 metros o más.
text.en: 1.5 metres or more.

text.es: Una separación lateral suficiente para que el cruce pueda realizarse con seguridad y sin peligro.
text.en: Enough side-by-side distance so you can pass them safely and without any danger.

text.es: 1 metro o más.
text.en: 1 metre or more.

explanation.text:
12 Distances
12.4 Lateral separation
All drivers when passing or crossing other vehicles and users should always leave a sufficient (side) separation distance so as to avoid any likelihood of danger and potential impact. This is referred to as ‘lateral’ separation.
As a general rule, this lateral separation depends on:
The speed.
The state of the road.
The vehicles that are crossing or passing.
The weather and environmental conditions.
An adequate lateral separation distance should allow sufficient margin both to avoid a dangerous situation from occurring and additionally to allow for any potential steering deviation to correct or realign the vehicle.

question.es: ¿Qué debe tener especialmente en cuenta para dejar con el vehículo de delante una distancia que le permita, en caso de frenada brusca, detenerse con seguridad?
question.en: What should you specifically take into account to give the vehicle in front enough space to allow them to stop safely in the event of sudden braking?

text.es: La velocidad y las condiciones de adherencia y frenado.
text.en: Speed and grip and braking conditions.

text.es: La velocidad de circulación, únicamente.
text.en: Driving speed only.

text.es: Las condiciones climatológicas y el tipo de vehículo que nos sigue.
text.en: The weather conditions and the type of vehicle behind us.

explanation.text:
12 Distances
12.5 Safety distance
The
safety distance
is the
minimum space
that a driver should leave between their vehicle and the vehicle ahead of them. This should be
sufficient
and enable them to stop,
without impacting and colliding with the vehicle ahead of them
, in the case of hard or unexpected braking by the preceding vehicle (the vehicle ahead of them). For safety it should always be greater than the stopping distance of the vehicle.
Not respecting
the safety distance from the vehicle in front of you is the
main cause
of
rear-end crashes
.
This distance should be increased when travelling at higher speeds or in reduced visibility, or where the road has low adhesion qualities and when the driver is unsure of the locality or lacks experience.
Not maintaining the safety distance with the vehicle driving ahead of you can cost
4 points.

question.es: Conduce un turismo en esta autopista, ¿qué distancia debe mantener con el turismo que circula delante?
question.en: You are driving a car on this motorway. What distance should you keep from the car in front of you?

text.es: Una separación mínima de 50 metros.
text.en: A minimum separation of 50 metres.

text.es: La que permita detener el vehículo sin colisionar con él, tenga o no intención de adelantar.
text.en: A distance that allows you to stop the vehicle without colliding with it, whether or not you intend to overtake.

text.es: La que permita detener el vehículo en caso de frenado brusco, sin colisionar con él, si no tiene intención de adelantar.
text.en: The one that allows stopping the vehicle in case of sudden braking, without colliding with it, if there is no intention to overtake.

explanation.text:
12 Distances
12.5 Safety distance
Any driver of a vehicle driving behind another must leave space that allows them to stop without colliding in the event of sudden braking, taking into account, in particular, speed, grip and braking conditions. However, a group of cyclists does not need to keep this distance, paying close attention to avoid collisions.
When it is possible for vehicles behind you to overtake, then in addition to leaving a sufficient separation distance so that in case of sudden braking by the vehicle ahead of you – you don’t crash into the back of it, you should additionally leave a gap to allow overtaking vehicles to overtake safely. (Note: that his rule is not applicable to a group of cyclists travelling together.)
Vehicles with a
MAM greater than 3500 kgs,
vehicles and combinations / sets of
vehicles over 10m long,
must keep a
minimum safety distance of 50 m.
(Página 180 del manual 'Learning to drive')
12 Distances
12.5 Safety distance
The obligation to leave a safety distance where it is possible for the vehicle behind to overtake
is not applicable to the following circumstances:
In a built-up-area
(within town and cities etc.)
.
Where overtaking is forbidden.
Where there is
more than 1 lane
for the direction travelled
.
When
intense traffic
does not permit overtaking.

explanation.text:
12 Distances
12.4 Lateral separation
All drivers when passing or crossing other vehicles and users should always leave a sufficient (side) separation distance so as to avoid any likelihood of danger and potential impact. This is referred to as ‘lateral’ separation.
As a general rule, this lateral separation depends on:
The speed.
The state of the road.
The vehicles that are crossing or passing.
The weather and environmental conditions.
An adequate lateral separation distance should allow sufficient margin both to avoid a dangerous situation from occurring and additionally to allow for any potential steering deviation to correct or realign the vehicle.

After signalling the manoeuvre, and confirming that it is safe to undertake it – the next stage is to carry it out (execute the manoeuvre). This means adopting the correct position, the correct speed, and continually observing in order to ensure that no danger is caused to other road users.

Each manoeuvre involves variations although the basic principles are the same, dependant upon the manoeuvre there are differences in the execution stage.

1 Priority and Right of Way
The driver of a vehicle that is obligated to
give way
or
concede the right of passage
to another road user:

This means indicating his presence and movement by showing the
reduction of speed,

4 points
.

explanation.text:
Priorities, level crossings and tunnels
5 Narrow Sections
5.2 Narrowing section without signed priority
5
.2.1 Order of preference in the absence of road signs
The following explains the order of preference in the absence of road signs, signals or authorised persons, and applies to priority when different types of vehicles approach a narrow road section and it is necessary for one of the vehicles to reverse back to allow the other vehicle to pass. Under these circumstance priority is given as follows:
1.Special vehicles and those travelling under special regulations that exceed the established masses and dimensions as per the regulated rules of vehicles (MAM).
2. Set of vehicles-except those within point 4 below.
3. Vehicles pulled by animals.
4. Cars that tow a trailer of up to 750 kilograms MAM and camping vehicles.
5.Public transport vehicles-designed to transport passengers.
6. Lorries, tractive units and good vans and goods vehicles.
7. Car and vehicles derived from cars.
8. Special vehicles that do not exceed the mass or dimension established within the regulating laws; heavy quadricycles and light quadricycles.
9. Three wheeled vehicles, motorcycles with sidecar and three wheeled mopeds.
10. Motorcycles, two wheeled mopeds and bicycles.

explanation.text:
Safe driving
3 Road works
3.1 Signage in Sections Undergoing Roadworks or Maintenance Tasks
Areas of road works can present a potential danger due to the modification and change of traffic direction or routes. Any changes must be signalled and signed accordingly, normally by using cones and deviation, routemarking panels. These serve not only to mark the intended course but to also identify the area where the work is being carried out. It is important both for the drivers and work personnel that the route indicated is followed, so as not to endanger the safety of either.
During night time and adverse meteorological conditions the road works are marked and indicated by lights and reflective devices.

When two vehicles meet within a bend, both of which have their high beam headlights on, it is necessary for the vehicle that is taking the bend

explanation.text:
Safe driving
5 Driving in rain
5.1.1 Aquaplaning
Aquaplaning
(also referred to occasionally as ‘hydroplaning’) is a frightening phenomenon whereby a wedge (or film) of water builds up between the tyres and the road surface. The
depth of water
on the road may be
excessive for the grooves
of the tyre
to suitably displace it
, which may also be heightened because of an inadequate depth of tyre tread.
This causes the vehicle to feel like it is “gliding or sliding on the water”. The result is complete
loss of normal control by the driver.
(Página 228 del manual 'Learning to drive')
Safe driving
5 Driving in rain
5.1.1 Aquaplaning
Aquaplaning is caused by the accumulation of water on the road and by irregularities in its surface. Therefore, when it rains, it is necessary to pay
special attention
to
potholes
and areas in which
puddles
may occur.
This effect is more likely to occur with inappropriate speed and very wide or badly worn tyres.
One of the best solutions to avoid aquaplaning is to
reduce the speed
in the first instance, so that the tyres can displace the water and the wheels can retain contact with the road surface.

highest gear possible,

clutch slowly and smoothly

Travel at a
speed that is suited to the weather conditions

.

safety distance

brakes smoothly

When it is snowing or there is a covering of snow, there is the possibility that the driver will be dazzled (similar to when it is sunny) as the lights are reflected back off the snow. Road signs may become hidden – the line markings may not be visible and the vertical road signs may become covered in snow.

same precaution as travelling on snow
. This means that, similar to snow, there is a risk of sliding and skidding. Always operate the hand controls and foot controls smoothly.
Turn the steering wheel, gently as it is particularly sensitive and the steering will feel very light when driving on ice. This is because there is reduced grip (adhesion) between the tyres and icy road surface. Smoothly and progressively, operate the clutch, accelerator and brake.
It is better to raise the foot slowly off the accelerator in a bid to lose speed. Try to avoid using the brakes, and always brake gently where necessary, so as not to lose control of the car.

3 The fuel supply system – fuel to engine
3.1 Maintenance
To maintain an efficient engine it is fundamental that the fuel system is satisfactorily maintained. This means ensuring that:
The air filter is kept clean and adequately maintained. The more obstructed it becomes the higher the fuel consumption. It is necessary to periodically check the air filter, more frequently during the summer than during the winter and more so when travel has occurred in dusty locations or within cities. It should be replaced when it is excessively dirty or in accordance with the manufacturers guidelines.

explanation.text:
Mechanics and maintenance
8 Transmission system
Vehicles can have various drive arrangements:
Front wheel drive
: The driving wheels are located at the front. The advantage of front wheel drive is that all the main components are accommodated under the bonnet thus allowing maximum space within the car for the occupants, without floor bulges for the rear passengers. Using the front wheels for steering allows the driving force to act in the same direction as the wheel is pointing. Mostly, the engine is mounted transversely. This simplifies the transmission, with the clutch and the gearbox mounted in the main unit on the front axle.
Rear wheel drive:
The driving wheels are at the back. The normal layout in a rear wheel drive vehicle is, the engine and gearbox at the front and the differential behind.
Four-wheel drive:
The drive is distributed to all four wheels. (Also referred to as “x4” vehicles).

explanation.text:
Mechanics and maintenance
9 The steering system
9.1 Improvements in steering systems
9.1.2 Progressive power steering
This type of steering complements the previous one, adapting the stiffness of the steering to the vehicle’s speed.
By means of a series of sensors, the system is able to register the driver’s behaviour on the steering wheel, the vehicle’s running speed and the engine speed. Based on these parameters, an electrical control unit instantly calculates the torque assist level required at any given time.
When the car is stopped or moves very slowly, the effort required to move the steering wheel is reduced to a minimum. However, at higher speeds, the steering will be slightly stiffer, which provides a more precise control of the vehicle.

explanation.text:
Road traffic collisions
1 A public health problem
Moreover, in addition to the human drama, it is important to highlight the
enormous economic impact
(either directly or indirectly) that occurs as a result of a traffic collision.
Costs
derived from road traffic accidents are classified as
human, material, healthcare and administrative.
Human
costs include the loss of lives, productive capacity and physical and psychological suffering.
Material
costs consist of damages caused on vehicles and their loads as well as on the road and the environment.
Healthcare
costs comprise first aid, care and treatment of the wounded, rehabilitation and adaptations.
Administrative
costs hold those of police officers and firefighters and insurance and services management.
People believe that an accident has little effect on them but the cost is borne by taxpayers. The cost of vehicle insurance is also affected, as premiums are affected by collision data and the cost of accidents.
For these reasons, various international organisations, including the World Health Organisation (WHO), believe that road collisions are a priority public health problem throughout the world.
There is a serious need to work together to reduce the high numbers of dead and seriously injured on the roads.

explanation.text:
Road traffic collisions
2 Road traffic collisions can be avoided
With thought and knowledge it is possible to work out
where, when, how and why
collisions occur and therefore how to avoid them.
Certain circumstances related to the vehicle, the road and the environment but above all the driver, increase the likelihood of a road traffic collision or make the results of a collision much more serious. These circumstances are called
“risk factors”
and avoiding or minimising them reduces the possibility of being involved in a collision.
Some of these risk factors are fatigue, alcohol, excessive speed, ice or driving with a poorly maintained vehicle, particularly worn tyres.

question.es: ¿Qué factores intervienen en un accidente?

text.es: El factor humano, exclusivamente.

explanation.text:
Road traffic collisions
2 Road traffic collisions can be avoided
2.2 Factors involved in collisions
Generally, the factors that influence the occurrence of a traffic collision are varied, but always one or more of these factors are involved: the
vehicle, the road (& environment) and the driver.
Not all risk factors are equally important. Of every 100 collisions, only between
4 and 13 are due mainly to vehicle factors
(for example, a defective tyre or deficient brakes) and only
between 10 and 35 are due mainly to the road and related environment factors
(for example, when the roadway is wet and the vehicle loses control).
Most collisions,
between 70 and 90%, are due to the human factor
(for example, the driver becomes distracted, or speeds or is under the influence of alcohol etc).

explanation.text:
Road traffic collisions
2 Road traffic collisions can be avoided
2.3 The key: Reducing the risk
It is also possible to avoid many of the risk factors that are connected with the vehicle, the road or the environment.
In many collisions, the driver claims that the vehicle or road was an associated or main factor but the simple truth is that the driver could have behaved in a different way that would have avoided a collision. For example, if the driver had realised that the tyres were defective (by maintenance and inspection) they could have avoided the puncture (blow out) or if they had adopted an adequate speed and a safe distance when driving in the rain or snow, they could have avoided running into the vehicle ahead of them.
Proper maintenance and responsible driving reduces the chances that a “vehicle factor” or a “road factor” will be a cause of a collision.

RISK GROUPS
5 Pedestrians
5.1 Children
Some of these limitations of children are:
Limiting the field of vision.
When a child walks between parked cars the visual field can become 40% lower than that of an adult, due to their short stature. In addition, they also have problems with peripheral vision, which requires them to turn their head in order to see properly.
Hearing problems.
The under seven’ are not adequately able to locate sound by direction, so they have problems locating a vehicle and judging the direction it is approaching from. This requires the child to look both ways and to turn their head in order to locate the sound.

Lower level of attention.
Those under the age of ten do not usually pay sufficient attention to the aspect of safety, so they can be easily distracted near roads.
They tend to confuse “ee”with “e seen.”
When they see a vehicle, they may automatically think that the driver has also seen them.
Unaware of traffic regulations.
Children are often not aware of relevant road signs or the proper behaviour required when near or travelling on the road.
Children are especially vulnerable, since their small and developing stature is likely to be adversely affected by an impact, particularly in the region of the head or other vital parts of the body.

Young drivers

better condition of physical fitness,
have
better reflexes
and
skills
that are more
suited to driving.

limitations,
including
lack of experience
or
the tendency to take more risks.
There are many young people who drive safely and therefore have no increased risk of being involved in a collision than other older drivers.
However, in Spain each year hundreds of young people die in road traffic collisions, which are the
leading cause of death in the 15 to 29 year age group.

Accelerate gradually, gently pressing the pedal.
It is recommended that you use
first gear
only for
starting off
and pulling away, changing to second gear within a short period of time (within two-seconds or six metres).
In general, change gear as soon as possible and then accelerate
smoothly and progressively,
carrying out the changes in accordance with the following:
According to the revolution
Petrol

Diesel
Between 1.500 & 2.000 rpm

9.2 Accelerating and changing gears
These recommendations should be tailored to each particular case. If the vehicle carries a heavy load or is being driven on an upward or downward slope for example, you may
need to change gear a little earlier or a little later.
Sometimes,
there is no need to take the next consecutive gear
(1st  2nd  3rd  4th  5th), as gears can be missed if necessary; for example, in a downward slope it is possible to move from 3rd to 5th outright (1st  2nd  3rd  5th).
The automobile uses less fuel when
the highest gear that can be selected
is used; so if possible, it should be selected and the vehicle driven with the engine at
low revolutions.

adapting it to the road and traffic conditions. The continuous variation of speed will increase fuel consumption, and in heavy traffic, driver fatigue will occur.

Use the techniques of preventive driving:
drive always with anticipation and awareness, maintain an adequate safety distance and keep the field of vision as broad as possible, so as to be able see 2 or 3 vehicles in front.
Unnecessary stopping and starting and speed variations caused by the lack of foresight
and anticipation
increase consumption.

explanation.text:
Journeys and defensive and efficient driving
10 Factors affecting consumption
10.1 Air resistance
The majority of fuel consumed is used to overcome air (wind) resistance that acts against the advancing vehicle.
This means that anything that increases or changes the aerodynamics lines (the design) of a vehicle has a greater impact on consumption.
This is why
external accessories,
(roof racks, flaps and deflectors, etc.) increase the resistance of the vehicle and, therefore,
increase fuel consumption.
It is not advisable to leave
the roof rack on the vehicle
when it is empty and not being used.
It is preferable to carry the load in the boot, whenever possible and not on the roof rack.

This system reduces fuel consumption and the emission of greenhouse gases.
The system is activated automatically when starting the vehicle. When driving, the system stops the engine (stand-by) if the vehicle comes to a halt (traffic jams, traffic lights, etc.).

Public authorities may define

within their territory, which are continuous and apply
restrictions
on vehicle access, traffic and parking to improve air quality and mitigate greenhouse gas emissions, in accordance with the classification of vehicles by their level of emissions.
Low-emission zones shall be signposted with the vertical sign indicated below.
Low emission zones shall be signposted using vertical sign R-120, which prohibits access to vehicles based ontheir environmental badge or other established environmental criteria.
